title: Legion, a Bleeding Woman, and Jairus's Daughter
summary: Across the lake in Gentile territory, Jesus frees a man possessed by a legion of demons, who enter a herd of pigs that rush into the sea; the frightened townspeople ask Jesus to leave, and the healed man proclaims what Jesus has done throughout the Decapolis. Back on the Jewish side, Jairus begs Jesus to heal his dying daughter. On the way a woman who has bled for twelve years touches his cloak and is healed, and though word comes that the girl has died, Jesus takes her by the hand and raises her to life.
story:
At the end of chapter 4 the disciples asked who Jesus is, since even wind and sea obey him. Chapter 5 answers with three more displays of his authority, each over a power more desperate than the last: a host of demons, a chronic disease that no doctor could cure, and death itself. The storm on the lake gives way to a different kind of chaos in a man living among tombs, and the Greek uses the same pattern of fear after rescue: the disciples feared after the calm (4:41), and the townspeople fear when they see the man calm and clothed (5:15). Together with the storm, these stories form a sequence of four mighty works that show the reach of God's kingdom in Jesus over nature, spirits, sickness, and death.

The chapter also crosses boundaries. Jesus goes to Gentile land and back, touches and is touched by the unclean, and enters a house of mourning. The first episode ends with a Gentile sent to proclaim what Jesus has done, the first person in Mark sent out with that message; the second ends with a command to silence and the ordinary instruction to give the girl something to eat. The contrast of chapter 6 is already prepared: faith that reaches out to Jesus here, unbelief that keeps him at arm's length in his hometown there.
historical:
The eastern shore of the Sea of Galilee was largely Gentile territory belonging to the cities of the Decapolis, a group of Greek cities most of which lay east of the Jordan. Pompey freed them from Hasmonean Jewish rule when he reorganized the region in 63 BC, and Pliny the Elder lists ten of them (Natural History 5.74), including Scythopolis, Gadara, Hippos, Pella, and Gerasa, while noting that writers disagreed about the list. They were Greek in language, religion, and civic life, and their ruins, temples, theaters, and colonnaded streets still stand at Jerash and Beth-shan. Keeping pigs, which the law treated as unclean (Leviticus 11:7, Deuteronomy 14:8), was normal there, while the Mishnah forbids Jews to raise pigs anywhere (m. Bava Kamma 7:7). Pigs also carried a charge of persecution in Jewish memory: Antiochus IV ordered them sacrificed when he tried to abolish Judaism in 167 BC (1 Maccabees 1:47), and 2 Maccabees 6 and 7 tell of martyrs who died rather than eat pork.

Manuscripts differ over the region's name, reading Gerasenes, Gadarenes, or Gergesenes (see text). Gerasa, modern Jerash in Jordan, lay more than thirty miles southeast of the lake; Gadara, modern Umm Qais, about six miles southeast, with territory that probably reached the shore. In the third century Origen (Commentary on John 6.41) rejected both and preferred Gergesa, an old town by the lake with a steep slope pointed out as the place where the swine rushed down. In 1970 road builders on the eastern shore uncovered the remains at Kursi, where Vassilios Tzaferis excavated a large Byzantine monastery and, up the slope, a small chapel around a rock, evidently marking the traditional site of the miracle. Many scholars think Kursi preserves Origen's Gergesa.

The name Legion would have meant one thing anywhere in the Roman east: a unit of the Roman army, in the first century about five thousand infantry with a small cavalry force, the visible face of imperial power. The Tenth Legion, Fretensis, which fought in the war of AD 66 to 70 and was then garrisoned in Jerusalem, used a boar among its emblems, and tiles and bricks stamped with it have been found in the city. Ched Myers (Binding the Strong Man, 1988) and others read the exorcism as a coded picture of Rome driven into the sea; others think the name simply conveys overwhelming number, as the spirit itself explains (verse 9). Jairus, by contrast, is a synagogue leader (archisunagōgos) on the Jewish side of the lake. A Greek inscription found in Jerusalem in 1913 and usually dated before AD 70 records that Theodotus, a priest and archisunagōgos, son and grandson of archisunagōgoi, built a synagogue for the reading of the law and the teaching of the commandments, which shows the office's standing and that it could run in families.
cultural:
Tombs were caves or chambers cut into hillsides, and in Jewish law contact with a corpse, a bone, or a grave made a person unclean for seven days (Numbers 19:11-16). To live among them was to live permanently in the place of death and defilement. Isaiah had described a rebellious people “sitting among the graves, spending nights in secret places, eating the meat of pigs” (Isaiah 65:4), and the Greek Psalm 67:7 (68:6 in English Bibles) speaks of the rebellious who dwell in tombs. Mark's scene gathers every sign of uncleanness a Jewish hearer knew, an unclean spirit, tombs, pigs, and Gentile land, and Jesus walks into the middle of it. The chains and fetters show that the community had tried to restrain the man, and his crying out night and day and harming himself show a life in torment. In the ancient world knowing a spirit's name was thought to give power over it; spells in the Greek magical papyri adjure spirits by the names of gods, and one in the great Paris papyrus (PGM IV.3019) even invokes the god of the Hebrews, Jesus. Jesus asks the name, but his authority does not depend on it: he had already commanded the spirit to come out (verse 8).

The woman's condition made her ritually unclean under the law for as long as it lasted (Leviticus 15:25-27), along with anything she lay or sat on, and anyone who touched those things was unclean until evening. Susan Haber (Journal for the Study of the New Testament, 2003) and Amy-Jill Levine (1996) have cautioned against the common assumption that Jewish law made her an outcast banned from all society; purity rules governed approach to the temple and some contact, not whether she could live among neighbors, and Mark himself stresses her illness, her suffering, and her poverty rather than her impurity. Mark says she had spent everything on physicians and only grown worse; the Mishnah preserves a harsh proverb that the best of physicians is bound for Gehenna (m. Qiddushin 4:14), and the Babylonian Talmud records a string of folk remedies for a flow of blood (b. Shabbat 110a-b). Luke, traditionally a physician, softens the remark (Luke 8:43).

Mourning in a Jewish household began at once, with wailing, lament, and flute players; the Mishnah rules that even the poorest man in Israel must provide at least two flutes and one wailing woman for his wife's funeral (m. Ketubbot 4:4). The mourners' laughter shows that the girl was plainly dead. Talitha koum is Aramaic, the everyday language of Jewish Galilee: talitha, a diminutive meaning girl or little lamb, and koum, get up. Mark keeps the words and translates them for Greek-speaking readers, as he does elsewhere (3:17, 7:34, 14:36, 15:34). Calling the woman daughter gave her public standing before the crowd, and telling the parents to feed the girl returned her to ordinary life at her family's table.
literary:
The chapter has two main episodes, and the second is one of Mark's sandwich stories, a device James R. Edwards studied in a 1989 article: the raising of Jairus's daughter (verses 21 to 24 and 35 to 43) is interrupted by the healing of the bleeding woman (25 to 34), and each story interprets the other. Both involve a daughter, both involve the number twelve (years of illness, years of age), both involve touch and uncleanness, and both turn on faith in the face of hopelessness. The two women are opposites in every social respect: one is a named leader's child in a house full of mourners, the other an unnamed woman, alone and impoverished. The delay caused by the woman seems to cost Jairus his daughter, and Jesus' word to him, “Do not be afraid; just believe,” carries the lesson of the woman's faith directly into his crisis.

The Gerasene story is told at length (twenty verses) with vivid detail and in three movements: the encounter and exorcism (1-13), the reaction of the townspeople (14-17), and the commission of the healed man (18-20). The spirit's plea, the bargaining over where it may go, and the stampede give the story the shape of a battle in which the strong man is bound and his house plundered, as Jesus said in 3:27. The story also reverses Mark's usual pattern of secrecy. In Jewish Galilee Jesus commands silence (1:44, 5:43); in Gentile territory he sends the man to tell what the Lord has done, and the man tells what Jesus has done (19-20). Mark lets the reader notice the substitution.

The raising of Jairus's daughter is the first time Peter, James, and John alone go with Jesus, as they will on the mountain (9:2) and in Gethsemane (14:33). The scene closes a circle begun in the storm: fear and faith are set against each other in 4:40 and again in 5:36, and the chapter's last word of astonishment (ekstasis, verse 42) prepares for the unbelief that follows in Nazareth.

outline.t: A man possessed by Legion set free
The townspeople's fear and the healed man's witness
A woman healed by touching Jesus' cloak

doctrines.note: The unclean spirits recognize Jesus as “Son of the Most High God” and beg him not to torment them; they are many, organized, and destructive, but they cannot act without his permission (verse 13). The New Testament treats such powers as real and as already defeated in principle by the one who has bound the strong man (3:27).

The healed man begs to go with Jesus, but Jesus sends him home to tell his own people how much the Lord has done for him, and he proclaims it through the ten cities of the Decapolis (verses 19 and 20). He is the first person in Mark sent out with the news about Jesus, and he is a Gentile, a foretaste of the gospel preached to all nations (13:10). His message is simply his own story of mercy.

The same Greek verb (sōzō) means to save, heal, and make whole. Jairus asks that his daughter be saved and live (verse 23); the woman believes that touching Jesus will save her (verse 28); Jesus tells her that her faith has saved her and sends her in peace (verse 34). Rescue here reaches the whole person: body, mind, social standing, and relationship with God.

The woman's faith is hidden and mixed with something close to superstition, and Jairus's faith is shaken by news of death, yet Jesus honors both. He draws the woman's faith into the open and personal encounter, and he tells Jairus to keep believing when circumstances say it is too late.

Jesus calls death sleep, not because the girl was not dead but because for him death is not final, the language Daniel 12:2 uses of the resurrection and the New Testament uses of believers who have died (1 Thessalonians 4:14). Raising her restores her to mortal life; it anticipates the resurrection Christians confess, beginning with Jesus himself.

words.note: Akathartos, unclean. It occurs 32 times in the New Testament, eleven of them in Mark, almost always in the phrase unclean spirit, which Mark uses where Matthew and Luke more often say demon. The word comes from Israel's purity vocabulary (the Greek Old Testament uses it for unclean animals, Leviticus 11), and in Mark it marks spiritual evil as the opposite of the Holy Spirit and of the Holy One of God (1:24). In this chapter the unclean spirit, the tombs, and the pigs belong together.

Legeōn, legion, a Latin military word (legio) borrowed into Greek. It occurs four times in the New Testament: twice here (verses 9 and 15), in Luke 8:30, and in Matthew 26:53, where Jesus says he could ask his Father for more than twelve legions of angels. It is one of several Latin terms in Mark's Greek, alongside denarius (6:37), executioner (spekoulatōr, 6:27), and centurion (15:39), which some cite in support of a Roman origin for the Gospel. As a name it conveys a vast, organized, oppressive force.

Parakaleō, to call alongside, and so to beg, urge, exhort, or comfort. It occurs about 109 times in the New Testament, most often in Acts and Paul in the sense of exhort or comfort. In this chapter it appears five times, always as begging: the spirit begs not to be sent away (10), the demons beg to enter the pigs (12), the townspeople beg Jesus to leave (17), the healed man begs to go with him (18), and Jairus begs for his daughter (23). Everyone in the chapter pleads with Jesus, and what each one asks shows where they stand.

Mastix, whip or scourge, and by extension a torment or affliction. It occurs six times in the New Testament: literally of flogging (Acts 22:24, Hebrews 11:36) and figuratively of disease as a scourge (Mark 3:10, 5:29, 5:34, Luke 7:21). BDAG notes the figurative sense of a tormenting illness. Its use for the woman's condition, twice, names her twelve years as a punishment she did not deserve, and Jesus sends her away free of it (verse 34).

Dunamis, power, ability, and in the plural mighty works. It occurs about 119 times in the New Testament and ten times in Mark, where the plural is the ordinary word for miracles (6:2, 6:5, 6:14). In verse 30 Jesus knows that power has gone out from him. Mark describes it almost as a force, but Jesus refuses to let the healing remain impersonal: he searches the crowd until the woman comes forward and hears that it was her faith, and his word, that made her whole.

Sōzō, to save, rescue, heal, make whole. It occurs about 106 times in the New Testament and fifteen times in Mark, with a range from rescue from death (15:30-31) to healing (here, verses 23, 28, 34) to final salvation (8:35, 13:13). BDAG groups the healing uses under preserving or rescuing from a threat to life. In verse 34 Jesus uses the perfect tense, ‘your faith has saved you’, the same words he says to blind Bartimaeus (10:52), and the healing is sealed with a blessing of peace.

Pistis, faith, trust. It occurs about 243 times in the New Testament but only five times in Mark (2:5, 4:40, 5:34, 10:52, 11:22), where it is always trust directed toward Jesus or God in a moment of need. The disciples in the storm have none yet (4:40); the woman's faith reaches out and is named (5:34). Jesus directs attention away from the cloak to her trust in him, which is why he insists on meeting her face to face. Jairus hears the verb in the present imperative, keep believing (verse 36).

Koum, get up or arise, an Aramaic imperative transliterated into Greek, with talitha (G5008), girl. Both words occur only here in the New Testament. Mark translates the phrase and adds I say to you, and the command is simply the ordinary word for waking someone. Where Elijah and Elisha stretched themselves over dead children and prayed (1 Kings 17:21-22, 2 Kings 4:33-35), Jesus takes the girl's hand and speaks. Later manuscripts correct the form to koumi, the proper feminine (see text).

christ:
The chapter shows Jesus as Lord over every power that destroys human life. The unclean spirits call him “Son of the Most High God” and beg him not to torment them, recognizing their judge before the disciples have found words for who he is. Jesus binds the strong man and plunders his house, as he said in 3:27. When the healed man is told to proclaim how much the Lord has done for him, he goes and proclaims how much Jesus has done, which quietly identifies Jesus with the Lord, the God of Israel, whose mercy the man has received. The man then becomes the first missionary to the Gentile cities, a foretaste of the mission to the nations that Mark's readers were part of (13:10).

Jesus is not made unclean by tombs, pigs, bleeding, or death. Under the law uncleanness spread by contact; here life spreads from Jesus to the unclean, and the direction of contagion is reversed. Isaiah had pictured a rebellious people sitting among graves and eating pork (Isaiah 65:4); Jesus comes to such a place and leaves a man clothed and in his right mind. The woman touches the tassels of a man of Israel, and power goes out from him to heal her. The raising of the girl echoes Elijah and Elisha, who restored children to their mothers (1 Kings 17:17-24, 2 Kings 4:18-37), but Jesus acts by his own word rather than by prayer and effort, and he calls death sleep because he intends to wake her.

For Mark's readers, who knew of his cross and empty tomb, the story points beyond itself. The girl is raised to mortal life and will die again; Jesus will be raised to life that death cannot touch. The three disciples who see her rise will see his glory on the mountain and his anguish in Gethsemane, and they too will struggle to believe the news of his resurrection when it comes (Luke 24:11). The chapter shows who Jesus is and what his coming means: God's own power over the forces that wreck human lives, used in mercy for a tormented Gentile, a poor woman, and a frightened father.
interpretation:
Readers argued about the place of the Gerasene miracle from early on. Origen (Commentary on John 6.41) judged that neither Gerasa nor Gadara fit the story and preferred Gergesa, and the site at Kursi was venerated by the Byzantine period. Augustine (On the Morals of the Manichaeans 2.17) used the drowning of the pigs against the Manichaeans, who forbade killing animals, arguing that Christ showed by it that human beings do not share a common moral community with beasts. The bleeding woman had a long afterlife in devotion. Eusebius (Church History 7.18) reports a bronze statue at Caesarea Philippi of a woman kneeling before a man in a cloak, said to show her healing, which he saw himself, and the apocryphal Acts of Pilate (probably fourth century) gives her the name Bernice, in Latin Veronica, and has her testify for Jesus at his trial. That name later passed to the woman of the Western legend who wiped Jesus' face on the way to the cross, and Orthodox calendars commemorate Saint Veronica, the woman with the flow of blood, on July 12.

Modern criticism has argued chiefly about the exorcism. David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) read the story as legend, and Rudolf Bultmann (New Testament and Mythology, 1941) argued that belief in demons belongs to a mythical worldview that modern people cannot share. Historians have nonetheless treated exorcism as one of the best attested features of Jesus' ministry. The Jewish scholar Geza Vermes (Jesus the Jew, 1973) set Jesus beside the Galilean charismatic holy men Honi the Circle-Drawer and Hanina ben Dosa, and Graham Twelftree (Jesus the Exorcist, 1993) compared his exorcisms with others of the period and found them distinctive in their directness. Paul Hollenbach (Journal of the American Academy of Religion, 1981) read possession as, in part, a response to social and colonial oppression, and Ched Myers (1988) read Legion as a picture of Roman occupation. Richard Bauckham (Jesus and the Eyewitnesses, 2006) suggested that named characters such as Jairus were known figures in the early church who could vouch for their stories. Feminist and Jewish scholars, among them Susan Haber and Amy-Jill Levine, have corrected readings that turn the bleeding woman's story into an attack on Jewish purity law.

In liturgy the Revised Common Lectionary reads verses 21 to 43 in Year B (Proper 8), and the Roman Lectionary reads them on the thirteenth Sunday in Ordinary Time, with an option to read only the Jairus frame; the Gerasene story is read in Luke's version (Luke 8:26-39) in Year C. In art the raising of Jairus's daughter was the subject set for the Imperial Academy of Arts' gold medal in 1871, and Ilya Repin's version, which he said came alive for him only when he connected it with the death of his sister, won it and launched his career.
text:
The place name in verse 1 is the best-known difficulty. In Mark the earliest witnesses (Codex Sinaiticus in its original hand, Codex Vaticanus, Codex Bezae, and the Latin tradition) read ‘Gerasenes’, which modern versions follow. Codex Alexandrinus and most later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read ‘Gadarenes’, and a corrector of Sinaiticus and several other manuscripts read ‘Gergesenes’, the form Origen preferred. The best text of Luke (8:26) also reads Gerasenes, while the best text of Matthew (8:28) reads Gadarenes, and Matthew tells of two men. Scribes plainly tried to solve a geographical problem, and Mark's ‘region of the Gerasenes’ may simply use the best-known city's name for the district.

In verse 36 the earliest manuscripts read parakousas, which can mean either ‘overhearing’ (so the BSB, ESV, and NRSV) or ‘ignoring’ (so the RSV, ‘ignoring what they said’); both fit, and the second makes Jesus' refusal to accept the messengers' verdict explicit. Later manuscripts, followed by the King James Version, read akousas, ‘as soon as Jesus heard’. In verse 41 the earliest manuscripts read koum, the masculine form of the Aramaic imperative; later ones, followed by the KJV's ‘cumi’, read koumi, the correct feminine form for a girl. The shorter form is the harder reading and probably original; spoken Galilean Aramaic may have used the masculine form for both. Codex Bezae and a few Old Latin witnesses omit the name Jairus in verse 22, probably to match Matthew 9:18, which does not name him.

teach.big: Jesus has authority over every power that destroys human life, demons, disease, and death, and he uses it in mercy for the unclean, the forgotten, and the desperate who reach out to him in faith.

outline.t: No one is beyond Jesus' reach: he crosses into unclean territory to free a man everyone else could only chain.
People can prefer their losses to their Lord; the healed man's story becomes his mission among his own people.
A leader with standing comes to Jesus on his knees: need levels every rank.
Jesus will not leave faith anonymous; he turns a secret touch into a public healing and a restored daughter.
When the news says it is too late, Jesus says keep believing, and he speaks life into death with a word.

teach.pitfalls:
Several misreadings recur. The first treats the Gerasene story either as proof that every mental illness is demonic or as proof that the Gospels simply misdiagnosed mental illness. The text distinguishes illness and possession elsewhere (1:32-34, 6:13), and it does not license anyone to diagnose a neighbor. A second turns the bleeding woman into a picture of Judaism as cruel to women, as if Jesus were abolishing the purity laws. Mark does not say that, and Jewish and Christian scholars have shown how this reading distorts first-century Judaism. A third makes the woman's touch a technique, as if faith were a switch that releases power; Jesus deliberately moves her from a secret touch to a personal meeting.

Preachers should also avoid promising that enough faith will always heal or bring the dead back. The chapter gives signs of the kingdom, not a guarantee that every believer's child will recover. Jairus's faith was weak and shaken, and his daughter was raised; many faithful parents have prayed and lost their children. Teach the chapter as what it is, a revelation of who Jesus is and a foretaste of the resurrection, not as a formula for results. Finally, do not skip the townspeople: their fear of Jesus' disruptive power, and their preference for their pigs over their neighbor's sanity, belong to the story's point.
teach.pastoral: This chapter presses on many people at once. Families living with severe mental illness, self-harm, or addiction will hear the description of the man among the tombs; teach it with compassion, never suggesting that illness is a spiritual failure, and keep a path to real help visible (a doctor, a counselor, a crisis line) alongside the church's prayer. Women with chronic illness, infertility, or long medical debt will recognize the woman who spent everything and grew worse. Parents who have lost a child will hear the raising of Jairus's daughter differently from everyone else; do not use it to imply that their faith was too small, and let the chapter's hope point to the resurrection, which is the promise it foreshadows. Jesus' words to Jairus, “Do not be afraid; just believe,” should be offered as an invitation to trust, not as a rebuke to the grieving.

hard.q: Were the demoniacs of the Gospels possessed, or mentally ill people described in the language of their time?
hard.a:
The skeptical case is weighty. David Friedrich Strauss (The Life of Jesus, 1835) treated the Gospel exorcisms as legend shaped by Jewish belief, and Rudolf Bultmann (New Testament and Mythology, 1941) argued that demons belong to a mythical picture of the world that no one who relies on modern medicine can honestly hold. Many readers note that the symptoms described here (extraordinary strength, self-harm, living apart, crying out night and day) resemble conditions that psychiatry now names, and that other Gospel cases resemble epilepsy (9:17-27). Paul Hollenbach (1981) added a social reading: possession in colonized societies can be a way of expressing and surviving oppression, which fits a man in a land ruled by Rome who calls himself Legion.

Others respond on several levels. Historians of widely different convictions, among them the Jewish scholar Geza Vermes (Jesus the Jew, 1973) and Graham Twelftree (Jesus the Exorcist, 1993), agree that Jesus was known in his lifetime as an exorcist; the question is how to interpret what happened, not whether the reports are late inventions. The Gospels themselves distinguish sickness from possession (1:32-34, 6:13), so they were not simply labeling every illness as demonic. The New Testament as a whole assumes that evil spiritual powers are real, and many Christians around the world, and many pastors and physicians who deal with severe cases, hold that both kinds of affliction exist and can overlap. The churches that practice exorcism require careful medical and psychological assessment first; the Roman Catholic rite revised in 1999 instructs exorcists to distinguish possession from mental illness and to seek professional help when in doubt. What the text plainly shows, whatever one's view of the cause, is a man destroyed by forces beyond his control and restored by Jesus to his right mind.

hard.q: Why did Jesus allow the demons to destroy some two thousand pigs, and the owners' livelihood with them?
hard.a:
The objection was put memorably by Bertrand Russell in his lecture Why I Am Not a Christian (1927): it was not kind to the pigs to send the devils into them, and an omnipotent Jesus could simply have made the devils go away. Animal-welfare advocates and many ordinary readers feel the same, and others add the loss to the herders and owners, who were given no say. Critics have also doubted the story's historicity, calling a herd of two thousand implausibly large and the stampede a legendary flourish.

Responses differ. Augustine (On the Morals of the Manichaeans 2.17) answered the Manichaeans, who held all killing of animals to be sin, that Christ showed by this act that human beings and beasts do not form one moral community, a reading most modern Christians would state more gently. Many commentators stress that the demons, not Jesus, drive the herd to destruction; Jesus permits it, and the stampede shows visibly that the spirits had left the man and what they intended for him. Others read the scene symbolically: J. D. M. Derrett suggested that the drowning recalls Pharaoh's army in the sea (Exodus 15:4-5), and Ched Myers saw Roman power driven back into the sea, while Jewish hearers would have heard unclean spirits and unclean animals returning to the deep. A further response points to the townspeople, who ask Jesus to leave: the story itself asks the reader to weigh a man's sanity against a herd, as Jesus does in Matthew 12:12 (“How much more valuable is a man than a sheep”). The text does not fully explain Jesus' permission, and honest readers can acknowledge the difficulty while keeping the story's own focus on the man.

observe: How does Mark describe the man's life before he meets Jesus, and how is he described afterward (verse 15)?
What does each person or group in the chapter beg Jesus for, and what does he do with each request?
What does Jesus say to the woman, and what does he say to Jairus after the messengers arrive?
interpret: Why do you think the townspeople were afraid and asked Jesus to leave, when their neighbor had been healed?
Why did Jesus insist on finding the woman who touched him instead of letting her slip away healed?
How do the two stories of the woman and the girl interpret each other, and what does the delay add to Jairus's story?
apply: The healed man was sent home to tell his own people how much the Lord had done for him. Who are your own people, and what would it mean to tell them?
Is there a need you have kept hidden from Jesus and from others, as the woman tried to? What would it mean to bring it into the open?
Where are you hearing that it is too late, and what would it look like to keep believing there?
